sections.title: Advanced Understanding of Cause and Effect
sections.content: At Level 2, simply identifying the cause and effect is not enough. It is also necessary to evaluate whether the cause is actually strong enough to produce the given result. Sometimes events appear similar but may have different causes. Therefore, it is important to carefully examine logic, timing, and the scope of the impact.

sections.title: Analysis of Direct Causation
sections.content: In direct causation, there is a clear and logical relationship between the cause and the effect. However, at Level 2 it is necessary to verify whether the cause is sufficiently powerful to produce the effect. Example: The government implemented a strict new tax law. As a result, many companies hired more chartered accountants. Here the policy change can directly lead to increased employment.

sections.title: Corporate Ripples
sections.content: In the corporate world, an event affecting one company can influence another company. Example: Company A experiences a sharp decline in profit. After this, Company B's market share increases. There are two possibilities: customers moved from Company A to Company B due to A's weakness (effect), or Company B was already growing due to its own strategy (independent effect). The question requires identifying the correct relationship.

sections.title: Policy Effects
sections.content: Government or institutional policies can create several economic or social outcomes. Example: A new strict tax law is implemented. As a result, companies hire more tax experts and chartered accountants. Here the policy change logically creates new employment opportunities.

sections.title: Common Cause vs Independent Causes
sections.content: Sometimes two events appear similar but may actually arise from a single common cause. Example: Two banks fail at the same time. This may happen due to separate administrative failures (independent causes) or because of a nationwide economic recession (common cause). The question is to determine whether the events share a cause or have different causes.

sections.title: Evaluating Scope and Magnitude
sections.content: In Level 2 questions, it is important to check whether the impact of the cause matches the scale of the result. If a very small cause is used to explain a very large outcome, the relationship is likely incorrect. Example: A small rule change in a town is said to change the entire national economy. This would not be logically reasonable.

sections.title: Types of Questions Asked in Exams
sections.content: 1. Whether statement I can actually be the cause of statement II. 2. Whether both events arise from a third common cause. 3. Whether the events arise from independent causes. 4. Whether the strength of the cause is sufficient for the level of the result.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Assuming causation simply based on sequence of time. 2. Ignoring independent causes in corporate or economic situations. 3. Not comparing the strength of the cause with the scale of the result. 4. Assuming a common cause just because the topic appears similar.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: At Level 2, when identifying cause and effect, check three things: whether the cause can realistically produce the result, whether a common cause exists, and whether the events may arise from independent causes. In corporate, policy, and economic examples, the scope of logic and the magnitude of the effect are very important.

tricks.title: Scope Matching Trick
tricks.explanation: Compare the scale of the cause and the result. A small cause usually cannot explain a very large outcome.
tricks.example: A small store's sales dropped and it is claimed that the entire industry's profit declined. This reasoning is incorrect.

tricks.title: Corporate Ripple Check
tricks.explanation: If one company becomes weaker, competitor companies may benefit. However, also check whether the second company may have improved due to its own strategy.
tricks.example: Company A's profit declined and Company B's market share increased. Customers may have shifted to B.

tricks.title: Policy Impact Rule
tricks.explanation: Government rules or policies often directly influence economic behavior.
tricks.example: A new tax law was introduced and companies hired more tax experts.

tricks.title: Common Cause Detection
tricks.explanation: If two events occur simultaneously, check whether a larger external factor is influencing both.
tricks.example: Two banks failed at the same time. A possible cause could be a national economic recession.

tricks.title: Independent Cause Check
tricks.explanation: If two events have separate reasons behind them, linking them together would be incorrect.
tricks.example: Two companies are facing losses but one suffers due to poor management and the other due to low demand.

tricks.title: Magnitude Logic
tricks.explanation: The larger the result, the stronger or more influential the cause should be.
tricks.example: A minor rule change cannot transform the entire economy.

tricks.title: Hidden Cause Search
tricks.explanation: If the direct connection between two events is unclear, consider the possibility of a hidden cause.
tricks.example: People are buying more umbrellas and traffic is slow. The hidden cause may be rain.

tricks.title: Time Order Verification
tricks.explanation: The cause must always occur before the effect.
tricks.example: The government changed a regulation and afterwards companies modified their policies.

tricks.title: Business Logic Trick
tricks.explanation: In corporate questions, consider market competition and customer behavior.
tricks.example: If one company stops producing a product, customers may move to a competing company.

tricks.title: Overthinking Avoidance
tricks.explanation: If a strong logical connection exists between the cause and effect, accept it without searching for unnecessary complexity.
tricks.example: A new tax rule was introduced and companies hired tax specialists.
